Q: Git "objects/[0-9a-f][0-9a-f]/" is not using the first two characters of the sha1 object name A:

Those objects are zlib compressed. If you deflate the compressed object before computing the sha1sum, then you will see the correct hash correspondence. Note that the 40 digit sha1 will be split into a two-digit subdirectory name and a 38 digit filename.

Here is an example:

$ git init .
Initialized empty Git repository in /private/tmp/g/.git/
$ echo "hello world" > myfile
$ git add myfile 
$ zlib-flate -uncompress < .git/objects/3b/18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad | sha1sum
3b18e512dba79e4c8300dd08aeb37f8e728b8dad  -

Q: Finding out what characters a given font supports A:

Janus' fonttools answer is very helpful, but I found the tuple building a bit confusing. Here's a solution that builds a dict for all characters found in the font. It also excludes non-printing and control characters.

import sys

# To get fontTools:
#   pip install fonttools
from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
from fontTools.unicode import Unicode

font_file = sys.argv[1]

with TTFont(
    font_file, 0, allowVID=0, ignoreDecompileErrors=True, fontNumber=-1
) as font:
    print("Loading font", font_file)
    chars = {}
    for x in font["cmap"].tables:
        for c in x.cmap.items():
            codepoint, name = c
            if (
                codepoint <= 0x1F  # Non printing
                or 0x7F <= codepoint <= 0x9F  # Control Characters
            ):
                continue
            chars[codepoint] = name

# Now you have a dictionary of all codepoints (utf number code) to unicode label.
for codepoint, name in chars.items():
    # `name` comes from the font and may be inaccurate,
    # so use Unicode lookup for labels:
    name = Unicode[codepoint]
    print(f"0x{codepoint:x}: {name}")

> python font.py Inconsolata-Regular.ttf

Loading font Inconsolata-Regular.ttf
0x20: SPACE
0x21: EXCLAMATION MARK
0x22: QUOTATION MARK
0x23: NUMBER SIGN
0x24: DOLLAR SIGN
0x25: PERCENT SIGN
...

Q: Create variable in R for if X at t(i) is different at t(i+1) A:

For your desired wide output, you can treat your status values as logical values e.g.:

testdata$status == "Yes"
# [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

When applying arithmetic to these values, R will coerce TRUE to 1 and FALSE to 0. So you can do something like:

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Starting with long data
testdata %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = id,
    names_from = year,
    values_from = status,
    names_prefix = "status"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    change2016 = (status2016 == "Yes") - (status2015 == "Yes")
    )

# # A tibble: 3 × 4
#   id    status2015 status2016 change2016
#   <chr> <chr>      <chr>           <int>
# 1 1     No         Yes                 1
# 2 2     Yes        Yes                 0
# 3 3     Yes        No                 -1

# Starting with wide data
testdata %>%
  mutate(
    change2016 = (status2016 == "Yes") - (status2015 == "Yes")
  )

Thanks to @M--, here's how to apply the same logic if you're starting with the long format version of your data:

testdata %>% 
  mutate(
    change2016 = ifelse(year == 2016, (status == "Yes") - (status == "Yes")[year == 2015], NA),
    .by = id
    )

#   id year status change2016
# 1  1 2015     No         NA
# 2  1 2016    Yes          1
# 3  2 2015    Yes         NA
# 4  2 2016    Yes          0
# 5  3 2015    Yes         NA
# 6  3 2016     No         -1

Q: Use FFmpeg to add text subtitles A:

This is the reason why Matroska (MKV) is such a good container, especially now that it's mature:

mkvmerge -o output.mkv video.mp4 subtitle.srt
